about: Searches of one corpus. The corpus: `conversations` ({id, title?, summary_title?, summary_text?, incognito?}); `rounds` ({conversation_id, idx, user_text, assistant_text, at}, recorded in this order, idx counting from 1 in each conversation, whose last_active_at is its latest round's `at`); and `facts` ({id, text, topic, recorded_at, valid_until?, conversation_id?, superseded_by?}, superseded when superseded_by is set). A field left out is null. An incognito conversation's rounds are recorded first, as any other's; marking it then deletes them and its summary, and keeps its title. Some text is written decomposed (NFD) or with Arabic harakat on purpose. Each case gives `query` and, optionally, `from_date` and `to_date` (YYYY-MM-DD, both included), `limit` (8 when left out), `timezone` and `exclude_conversation` (whose rounds, and the facts drawn from it, are left out). `expect` is the hits of search(...) with them, best first, a fact by its id and a round as r:<conversation_id>:<idx>; `expect_results`, where given, is the search_memory result's `results` for the same hits: {date, conversation, kind, text}, where conversation is the title of the hit's conversation, else its summary's title, else "" ("" too for a fact drawn from an incognito one). A case without `timezone` runs in UTC; with one, each day (the date window's and each hit's date) is a day in that IANA zone. Text is matched by its index tokens: normalise_for_index's text (NFKC, casefolded, combining marks removed, each CJK or Thai character set apart) as unicode61 with remove_diacritics 2 parts it, runs of letters, numbers and private-use characters, a Latin letter without its diacritics. A query's terms are its index tokens, each once, in order: a run of n CJK or Thai characters written together gives its n - 1 overlapping bigrams, matched whole, one in word_lists.json's cjk_stop_bigrams left out (a run of one is a term of one); any other token is a word, matched as a prefix of a token, unless it is in word_lists.json's stop_words or is a single character; at most 12 words and 24 CJK or Thai terms. A text matches when it holds any term; a query with no terms finds nothing. Facts and rounds are ranked apart, each by FTS5's bm25 (k1 1.2, b 0.75, an IDF at or under 0 counting as 1e-6), then fused by reciprocal rank fusion (k 60). A tie within a list goes to the newer, then to the one added later; a tie in fusion goes to the newer, then to the fact. Orders are pinned only where scores are far apart or tie exactly. Superseded facts count only when nothing else matches. A fact shows its text whole, after "(until YYYY-MM-DD) " when it has a valid_until. A round shows "User: " and its user_text, a line break, and "Assistant: " and its assistant_text (a side with no text left out), whole when that is at most 600 code points; else an excerpt around the match, cut in code points, so a long round leaves room for the other hits. The match is the first place in that text a term matches, sought with the two labels blanked, so "use" never matches "User". The window starts 300 before the match's first code point (at 0 when nothing matches), clamped so 600 fit. A start that doesn't follow whitespace moves forward to just past the next whitespace, never past the match; an end that isn't on whitespace moves back to the last whitespace, never before the match's end. The cut text is stripped. A cut start gets an ellipsis (U+2026), a space and the label of the side the stripped text begins in ("… Assistant: "), the label left out when that text begins with it; a cut end gets an ellipsis. When the reply holds matches that end after that window, a second window shows the best of them: of the reply's matches that end after the first window, the one from whose start the most distinct terms match within 360 code points, the earliest on a tie; those matches, from its start to the furthest one's end, are centred in 360 code points, clamped to the reply's own text and to the round's end, the cuts moved off words as above, around those matches. It follows the first window's stripped text, in place of that window's closing ellipsis, as a space, an ellipsis, a space, "Assistant: " and its own stripped text, with an ellipsis when it is cut before the round's end. A second window that starts at or before the first window's end joins it: one window from the first's start to the second's end. So an excerpt is at most 988 code points. `tool_cases` are search_memory calls: `arguments` as the engine sends them (null for one left out), with an optional `timezone` and `exclude_conversation`, and `expect`, the whole result, or `expect_count`, how many results it holds where their order isn't pinned. A call gets its limit kept within 8 to 20, or 12 when it gives none. When a call's dates match nothing, the search runs again without them, and the result's `note` is "nothing matched on those dates, so these results are from any date". A result over 12,000 code points drops results from the end, and "truncated" ends its note ("; " between two). Python's MemoryStore.search and MemoryStore.search_result_json replay every case on each backend (talk2view-python, tests/test_contract_memory.py).

rounds.user_text: Talked about the marathon route, the weather forecast, the water stations along the course and where the family would stand to cheer.
rounds.assistant_text: Sounds like a big day for everyone.

rounds.user_text: Give me a packing list for the glacier hike.
rounds.assistant_text: Here is a packing list for the glacier hike, roughly in the order you will need things. Start with layers: a thin merino base layer, a warm fleece, a light down jacket and a waterproof shell with a hood. Pack waterproof trousers, two pairs of wool socks and a spare pair in a dry bag. Wear stiff leather boots that are already broken in, and bring gaiters to keep snow out of them. For your hands, bring thin liner gloves and thick insulated mittens. Protect your eyes with glacier glasses and your skin with sunscreen and lip balm, because the light off the ice is strong. Bring a headlamp with fresh batteries, a paper map, a compass and a fully charged phone. Take two litres of water and plenty of snacks, such as nuts, dried fruit and chocolate. The guide will lend you a harness and a helmet, but bring your own crampons if they fit your boots, and practise putting them on at home first. Finally, pack a small first aid kit, blister plasters, a whistle and a foil blanket. Leave a note of your route and your expected return time with someone at the hut, and check the weather forecast the evening before you set off. If the forecast looks poor, the guide may move the hike to another day, so keep the following morning free as well. Bring some money for the hut, a book for the evening and earplugs, since the bunk rooms are shared.

rounds.user_text: What should I pack for a week in Iceland in March?
rounds.assistant_text: March in Iceland is still winter, so plan for cold, wind and short days, and for weather that changes several times in an afternoon. Daylight runs from about eight in the morning to seven in the evening, and the temperature in Reykjavik hovers around freezing, colder inland and up on the glaciers. Roads in the north may close for a day after a storm, so leave some slack in the plan and look up the road conditions each morning before you set off. Pack for warmth first: a thin merino base layer under a fleece keeps you warm without bulk, and a windproof shell matters more than the cold itself. Bring a woollen hat that covers your ears, warm gloves and a neck gaiter. Waterproof hiking boots with a good grip are worth it, because the paths to the waterfalls are icy, and slip-on ice cleats help on the steepest ones. Pack a swimsuit too. For the rental, a phone mount and a charging lead save a lot of fumbling, and a paper map is a good backup where the signal drops out. Petrol stations are far apart in the east, so fill up whenever the tank is half empty. Food is expensive, so a refillable bottle and a few snacks from the supermarket go a long way; the tap water is excellent everywhere. Keep a small torch in your pocket for the dark mornings. The best part of a winter trip is the hot water: after a day at the Geysir geothermal area, soak in a pool, where a swimsuit, a towel and flip-flops are all you need. Most towns in Iceland have one, open until late in the evening.
